result.question: Why did Awadh emerge as one of the most intense centres of the Revolt of 1857? Examine the grievances of different social groups there. (Answer in 250 words)

directives.meaning: Look into the issue in detail: its causes, effects and implications.

sentences.text: The Revolt of 1857 began as a sepoy mutiny at Meerut on 10 May 1857.
In Awadh it became a popular uprising against firangi raj in which prince, taluqdar, peasant and sepoy fought together.
Political humiliation: The Subsidiary Alliance, devised by Lord Dalhousie, was imposed on Awadh in 1801 and left the Nawab without his own army.
In 1856 Awadh was annexed on the plea of misgovernment, and the popular Nawab Wajid Ali Shah was exiled to Calcutta.
His exile cost musicians, poets, artisans and court officials their livelihood.
Taluqdars: The Summary Settlement of 1856 regarded the taluqdars as the rightful owners of the land and left their estates intact.
The taluqdars were also disarmed and their forts destroyed, and many of them joined Begum Hazrat Mahal in Lucknow.
Peasants: Without the patronage of the taluqdars, peasants were directly exposed to over-assessment and inflexible revenue collection.
Sepoys: Awadh was called the nursery of the Bengal Army, so sepoy grievances over low pay, difficulty in getting leave and racial abuse by officers travelled back to their villages.
The rumour that the cartridges of the new Enfield rifle were greased with the fat of cows and pigs became the immediate trigger.
Leadership: Rebels in Lucknow hailed Birjis Qadr, the young son of the Nawab, as their leader.
Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah fought in the Battle of Chinhat, where British forces under Henry Lawrence were defeated.
Resistance in Awadh lasted the longest, and Lucknow was recaptured by the British only in March 1858.
Awadh shows how shared grievances turned a mutiny into a people's revolt, later remembered by nationalists as the First War of Independence.
